Key points: • Q2 beat & raise across revenue, margins, and EBITDA • 26 new Electron/HASTE missions → launch backlog now exceeds 90 • Total backlog of ~$2.4B (+$800M incremental) • Space Systems and defense awards are accelerating • Neutron is expected to be pad-ready in Q4’26, while the Iridium + GHOST strategy remains on track

BofA downgraded $APP to Neutral, with a $400 price target (Omar Dessouky). Main reasons: • The previously expected 3–5% Q/Q growth from self-learning is no longer clear • Q2 growth appears to have been driven more by engineer-directed improvements • Given its high market share (roughly 2x its competitor’s), the long-term 30% Y/Y revenue growth target is at risk

Everyone Is Watching the Robots. I'm Watching the Chips Inside Them. China shipped more than 97% of the world's humanoid robots in the first half of 2026. Global shipments came to about 19,100 units, up from 5,100 a year earlier. AgiBot took 8,400 of them, Unitree 5,900. Tesla, Figure and Agility are nowhere close. That number is impressive. It is also the wrong thing to focus on if you invest in US equities. The robots are being assembled in China. The question that matters for a portfolio is what goes inside them. What is actually in a humanoid A production humanoid contains roughly 1,000 to 2,000 semiconductors, about ten times an industrial robot. Most people assume the AI chip is the story. By volume it is not. The inference processor is the single most expensive line in the bill of materials, but only 1-3% of the device count. The other 97-99% is analog and mixed-signal: motor drive transistors, gate drivers, position encoders, current-sense amplifiers, battery monitors, power regulators, IMUs, force-sensing chains. A humanoid has 40+ joint drives and 225-470 sensor devices. Every one needs conditioning and control. So there are two very different businesses here. The brain.NVIDIA's Jetson Thor is the reference platform: Blackwell GPU, 128GB of LPDDR5X at 273GB/s, 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS inside a 130-watt envelope. Production modules run $2,999 in 1,000-unit lots. Qualcomm launched Dragonwing IQ10 at CES 2026 for full-size humanoids. Both American. The body.Texas Instruments and Analog Devices sit in dominant positions across multiple layers of the stack. Infineon, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, NXP, Microchip and Renesas fill the rest. Renesas now publishes a complete humanoid reference design: nine-axis motor control, body controller, vision, battery management, all in one configuration. On memory, this is where I see people get it wrong. Humanoids do not use HBM. They use LPDDR5X plus NAND storage. Micron's CEO says a humanoid carries about ten times the memory of an average L2+ vehicle. Directionally right, but run the numbers. 500,000 robots in 2030 at 128GB each is 64 petabytes of DRAM. Even at 1TB per robot it is half an exabyte, against an industry shipping hundreds. Robots are not the memory cycle. They are an option on the back end of it. The numbers nobody quotes Silicon content per humanoid is $1,400-3,000, depending on whether you take UBS or Morgan Stanley. Multiply by 19,100 units and the entire global humanoid chip market in the first half of 2026 was $27-57 million. NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 revenue was $215.9 billion. The forecasts run wide. Smart Analytics Global sees 60,000 units this year and 500,000 by 2030, producing around $3 billion of robot revenue. Morgan Stanley models a $5 trillion market by 2050, with robotics semiconductor demand rising from $2.2 billion in 2025 to $1.8 trillion. UBS puts that same 2050 chip TAM at $177 billion. A tenfold gap between two banks tells you these are assumptions, not forecasts. How this shows up in earnings It doesn't, yet. No large chipmaker reports humanoid revenue separately because there is nothing to report. NVIDIA's robotics business was around 1% of sales, and from fiscal 2027 it is folded into a combined Edge Computing segment. TI, ADI and Infineon book it inside industrial. This is a design-win cycle, not a revenue cycle. The harvest is 2029-2032. The risk nobody prices If 97% of robots are Chinese, the chip decision is Chinese too. AgiBot is working with domestic AI chip firms. Huawei is supplying Ascend and Kunpeng to UBTech. Rockchip's RK3588 already ships in several Chinese humanoids. Meanwhile the FCC has added Chinese humanoids to its covered list, blocking new authorizations. The brain layer is the most exposed, because that is exactly what China is trying to replace. The analog and control layer is harder to copy and harder to displace. That is where I would rather own the exposure.

$NVDA + Wall Street giants (Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock GIP, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR) are joining forces on a $500 billion AI infrastructure financing package. According to the FT, the fund will support chips, power generation, and data centers. The deal could be announced as early as today. With Big Tech’s AI spending set to surpass $730 billion this year, private capital is stepping in. $NVDA shares fell 3%+ on the news.

Jefferies downgraded $AAPL to Underperform. The price target was lowered from $285.56 to $263.66. Analyst Edison Lee: • According to supply chain checks, the “all-glass iPhone” (September 2027) has been canceled due to low yields. • A major setback to Apple’s efforts to introduce more expensive iPhones amid high memory costs. • FY28/29 EPS estimates were cut by 2.1% / 3.4%. • The new DCF target implies 16% downside. In addition, Apple increased trade-in values by 5% in the U.S. and ~2% in Europe → this could drive early demand for the iPhone 17, but may put further pressure on iPhone 18 sales. #AAPL #Apple #Jefferies

Intel’s $15 Billion Stock Offering: A Strategic Move in the AI Era Intel $INTC announced on August 10, 2026 that it plans to raise $15 billion through a new common stock offering. Underwriters also have an option to purchase an additional $2.25 billion, bringing the potential total to $17.25 billion. At first glance, this looks negative. New shares mean dilution for existing shareholders. But the reason Intel is raising the money matters. The proceeds will mainly go toward capital expenditures and working capital, including new fabs, manufacturing equipment, cleanroom capacity, and securing wafer, substrate and memory supplies. Intel’s 2026 CapEx is already above $20 billion, and spending is expected to increase further in 2027. The company wants to fund this investment while keeping its balance sheet strong and maintaining its investment-grade credit rating. Why Now? AI is creating a huge demand for computing and advanced semiconductor capacity. Intel is trying to take advantage of that by expanding beyond its traditional CPU business into data center AI, custom silicon, advanced packaging and foundry services. Three areas stand out: Physical AI: Robotics, autonomous systems and AI that interacts with the physical world. Custom silicon: Specialized chips designed for the needs of major technology companies. Advanced packaging: Combining different chips and components to improve performance and efficiency. All of these require significant manufacturing capacity and capital. Intel’s Advantage One of Intel’s biggest advantages is its ability to manufacture advanced chips in the U.S. The 18A process is entering production, while 14A is targeted for high-volume production in 2028. This is strategically important. Most of the world’s leading-edge chip manufacturing is still concentrated in Asia, while governments and major customers increasingly want more domestic production. Intel is trying to position itself as a key part of that shift. The Bigger Opportunity: Foundry The foundry business could be the biggest long-term opportunity. Intel has traditionally designed and manufactured its own processors. Now it wants to manufacture chips for other companies as well. If Intel can scale this business, it could become a serious U.S.-based alternative to TSMC and Samsung, especially as demand for custom AI chips grows. The Cost The downside is obvious: dilution. Existing shareholders will own a smaller percentage of the company. And there is no guarantee that Intel’s massive investments will generate the expected returns. The foundry business is also extremely competitive, with TSMC remaining the benchmark. So the $15 billion raise is not automatically bullish. What matters is how efficiently Intel uses the capital. Bottom Line I see this as negative in the short term but potentially strategic in the long term. Intel is essentially choosing to accept some dilution today in exchange for stronger manufacturing capacity, a stronger balance sheet and a bigger role in the AI semiconductor supply chain. The real question isn’t why Intel is raising $15 billion. It’s how much value Intel can create with that $15 billion between 2027 and 2030. If the investments work, today’s dilution could end up being a relatively small price to pay for long-term growth. If they don’t, shareholders will simply own a smaller piece of a company that still hasn’t solved its biggest problems. For now, Intel is making a big bet on AI, advanced manufacturing and U.S.-based semiconductor production.
